viNames.name: Cá xiêm / cá chọi (tên chung của loài)

origin.fact: Comes from the Super Delta, a large-finned tail type that US breeders Peter Göettner and Paris Jones developed around 1980.
Frenchman Guy Delaval imported Super Delta offspring in 1984 and by 1987 had bred fish whose tail spread 180°. Before that, tails spread about 160° at most.
In the early 1990s, French breeders Laurent Chenot and Rajiv Massilamoni kept the line going. They crossed it with an American melano doubletail male, which produced the key fish R39.
US breeder Jeff Wilson named the fish 'halfmoons' in 1991. In 1993 a halfmoon called CHENMASWIL, shown by Chenot, Massilamoni and Wilson, won Best of Show at the IBC show in Tampa, Florida.
Vietnamese shop articles say Betta Halfmoon is mainly bred in Thailand.

looks.fact: When fully flared, the caudal (tail) fin spreads to 180° in a D-shaped half circle.

A good fish has a tail that opens a full 180° with straight outer edges. A curved edge or a smaller spread means it is not a halfmoon. The fin rays should branch many times, and the dorsal fin should be large, straight-edged and held up.
Hobbyists also judge the dorsal fin, the anal fin and how pure the colour is, not just the tail. IBC standards are the suggested benchmark.
Fish whose tail spreads less than 180° are usually called super deltas.
Comes in many colours, such as red, purple, blue and platinum.

lines.fact: Over-halfmoon (OHM): the tail spreads more than 180°.
Halfmoons are also bred with different amounts of ray branching: 4-ray, 8-ray and 16-ray.
Rosetail: a halfmoon with extra ray branching, which gives the tail a ruffled edge. Feathertail is the most extreme form. Masillamoni and Chenot developed it around 1989.
Halfmoon plakat (HMPK): combines the short fins of a plakat with the 180° spread of a halfmoon.
Vietnamese shops sell colour forms such as Rồng đỏ (red dragon), Nemo (orange, white and black) and solid black.

keeping.fact: Keep only one male per tank, because males fight. Tankmates should be peaceful fish that do not nip fins.
At least 5 gallons (about 19 L) is advised. Small unfiltered plastic bowls are not.
A minimum tank of about 4 US gallons (about 15 L).
A carnivore: feed quality betta pellets or flakes, plus frozen or freeze-dried bloodworms and brine shrimp.
Vietnamese keepers feed tubifex worms, mosquito larvae, boobo and pellets once or twice a day. They keep bettas in small tanks without aeration and avoid sharp decorations.
Dirty water shrinks or rots the fins, and tap-water chlorine can 'burn' them. Change water often and remove chlorine first.

breeding.fact: Breeds like any Betta splendens. The male fertilises the eggs, and a female ready to spawn has a round belly and a white spot at the vent.
Does not breed true: the halfmoon tail comes from several genes together. A good HM×HM pair usually gives only 10–30% halfmoon fry, and very good lines give 50–60%.
The best pairing is two good halfmoons from the same line. A super delta pair from a halfmoon line can also throw some halfmoons. Females should have rays that branch at least 3–4 times.
The early French lines became so inbred that males stopped building nests and no longer wrapped around females when spawning.
Early rosetails that showed up in halfmoon spawns could not spawn and were weaker than other halfmoons.

health.fact: Heavy, highly branched tails can tire the fish. The rays may break and the tail can collapse, and some fish bite their own tails, which raises the risk of fin rot.
Very finned fish (halfmoon, rosetail, feathertail) are said to live shorter lives than ordinary splendens or plakats.
Do not breed fish with a hunched back or that bite their own tails, because these traits can be passed on.

buying.fact: Buy from serious breeders. Choose males about 3–6 months old and ask to see photos of the parents or siblings.
Be careful: many fish sold as 'halfmoon' are really deltas or super deltas. Check that the tail flares to a full 180° with straight edges.

controversy.fact: Aquariadise argues against buying rosetail and other extreme-finned halfmoons. It says breeders picked fins over health and overlooked faults such as poor scales, and that most breeders see these fish as weaker.
The 1993 contest that started the halfmoon craze is still debated, and breeders disagree about how much credit Göettner deserves compared with the French breeders.
